solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Destructive phenomenon which could be rife?

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: its first half says shake up the letters of its second half, which then come out as this word

explanation.surface: A question about some destructive event that might spread everywhere, rife in the sense of widespread.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer is the clue to 'rife'. WILD signals an anagram, and FIRE rearranged gives RIFE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire raging out of control across open country is a natural disaster that destroys everything in its path.

clue.text: Addict to make no gains at all?

parts.note: to make money is to win it
nothing at all, the round letter O standing for zero

explanation.surface: A wry question whether being hooked on something means never getting ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'win nothing' is the reading: WIN plus O for zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A wino is a habitual drinker of cheap wine, so someone addicted to alcohol.

clue.text: This cryptically suggests I role play

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: LOOK gives LO, BACK turns it round to OL, and IN ANGER puts that inside IRE, spelling these two words

explanation.surface: An actor announcing a turn at role play, which the clue says the answer hints at cryptically.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer is a clue whose solution is 'I role'. LO means look, 'back' turns it round, and IRE is anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Look Back in Anger is John Osborne's 1956 stage drama, the famous 'angry young man' work of British theatre.

clue.text: Throwing something on the ground

definitions.meaning: ... someone is knocking them down or utterly confusing them, as in 'a ... question'
the boards, tiles or carpet laid over a floor

explanation.surface: Tossing an object down onto the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the floor: to floor is to throw down or baffle, and the material laid on a floor is its covering.

clue.text: Lots of leaves picked up in French city

indicators.note: something picked up by the ear is heard, so the word for many sheets is said aloud

parts.note: reams are large quantities of paper sheets

explanation.surface: Plenty of leaves gathered up from the ground somewhere in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' means sheets of paper, not foliage; the name of the city in Champagne is pronounced in English like the word for paper quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: Reims is a cathedral city in north-eastern France, capital of the champagne trade.

clue.text: Take off special clothing close by university

indicators.note: one piece wraps around another as clothes wrap a body

parts.note: the close of something is its end

explanation.surface: Removing particular clothes somewhere near a university campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' looks like undressing, but it means a parody; 'close' is the noun, an ending, not 'near'.
explanation.definitionFit: A send-up is a mocking imitation, the same as a take-off of someone.

clue.text: Save queen coming out of passage

indicators.note: the queen's letter leaves the passage, so it is removed

parts.note: an excerpt is a passage taken from a text
R is from Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A rescue of a queen emerging from a corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage' suggests a corridor but means a piece of writing; 'Save' is the old preposition, not rescue.
explanation.definitionFit: Save in the sense 'all save one' is a preposition meaning apart from or but.

clue.text: Like some weapons with handles joined

definitions.meaning: a ... shotgun has two barrels side by side
a ... surname links two family names with a hyphen

explanation.surface: Describes certain weapons whose grips have been fixed together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handles' is slang for names, so the second sense is a hyphenated surname, a classic British marker of posh families.
explanation.definitionFit: Two barrels make a gun double-barrelled, and two surnames hyphenated together make a double-barrelled name.

clue.text: Awful bore, spy film having trouble with viewing

indicators.note: an awful version of the words is a badly jumbled one, so they are rearranged

parts.note: pic is short for picture, a film

explanation.surface: A review panning a dull spy movie that had trouble with how it was shown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' looks like a verdict on the film but signals the anagram; 'viewing' is eyesight, not watching.
explanation.definitionFit: Presbyopia is the long-sightedness of age, so a presbyopic person struggles to see things close up.

clue.text: Mix in e-books making a breakthrough

indicators.note: one word is set in the middle of the other

parts.note: E as written, plus NT, the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
to merge things is to mix them together

explanation.surface: An instruction to blend something into electronic books to achieve a big advance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible's New Testament is a set of books, the usual crossword source for 'books'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something emergent is coming into view or being born, newly appearing as if breaking through a surface.

clue.text: Some lingo in an original form?

definitions.text: Some lingo in an original form?

indicators.note: put into a new, original shape, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A bit of language given a novel shape, which is exactly what the answer is.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: SOME LINGO rearranged gives the answer, which is itself new language.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologism is a newly coined word or expression, language appearing in a form never used before.

clue.text: Manage to smuggle uranium in car

indicators.note: smuggling carries something hidden inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to cope is to manage
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Succeeding in sneaking nuclear material inside a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupé is a two-door motor vehicle with a fixed roof.

clue.text: Back in quaint pub, giving a beam

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so its final letter is taken

parts.note: a bar is a pub or a room in one

explanation.surface: Back in an old-world inn, someone gives a smile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in quaint' is the end letter of quaint; 'beam' suggests a smile but means a structural member.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-bar is a metal girder whose cross-section is shaped like the letter T.

clue.text: Kit, maybe Chelsea kit coming off here

parts.note: a football team's kit is its strip
Chelsea is a London football club, one example

explanation.surface: A football shirt, say a Chelsea one, being pulled off in the changing room.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is a Premier League football club in London; a team's strip is its kit. Then 'kit coming off' points to undressing for an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip club is a venue where performers remove their clothes for customers.

clue.text: Son went off and felt intense passion

parts.note: food that went off decayed, or mouldered

explanation.surface: A son stormed off, overcome by strong feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went off' suggests departing but means rotting.
explanation.definitionFit: To smoulder is to burn without flame, and figuratively to harbour suppressed, intense desire or anger.

clue.text: Indication of speed in computer, feeling less hot at first

indicators.note: the hot letter comes ahead of the next piece

parts.note: a Mac is an Apple computer
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
numb means without feeling, so number means more numb

explanation.surface: A readout of speed on a computer, as someone grows less warm at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMBER here is 'more numb', not a figure; 'at first' puts H before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mach number is an aircraft's velocity expressed as a ratio of the speed of sound.

clue.text: Show some cheek: try ambitious project

parts.note: to moon is to bare one's buttocks, cheeks in the other sense
a shot is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: Be bold and have a go at a grand scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheek' means impudence on the surface, but bottom cheeks in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A moonshot is a hugely ambitious venture, after the space missions that aimed for the Moon.

clue.text: European runner set bar low at intervals

indicators.note: taking letters at regular gaps along the words, every other one

explanation.surface: An athlete from Europe who placed the high-jump bar low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' is crossword shorthand for a river, not an athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ebro is a major river in northern Spain flowing into the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Making too much stewed pear eaten by poet

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater

parts.note: Ovid was a Roman poet

indicators.note: fruit that is stewed is cooked down and broken up, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A poet earning too much while dining on stewed fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stewed' rearranges PEAR to ERPA, and 'eaten by' places it in OVID.
explanation.definitionFit: Overpaid means receiving more than is deserved, so earning too much.

clue.text: Place to study temperature: Kelvin or Celsius?

parts.note: uni is short for university
T is the symbol for temperature

explanation.surface: A laboratory question about which temperature scale to use.
explanation.definitionFit: Kelvin and Celsius are examples of measures, each a standard unit of temperature.

clue.text: One Italian who scored in game, then another

parts.note: monte is a card game, as in three-card monte
Verdi is another Italian composer, someone else who wrote scores

explanation.surface: An Italian footballer who scored in a match, followed by a team-mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scored' sounds like football but means wrote music.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudio Monteverdi was an Italian composer of early opera, someone who wrote musical scores.

clue.text: Fanatic snatching tip of rose bud

indicators.note: taking hold of something and keeping it inside

parts.note: a fiend is an enthusiast, as in a fitness fiend

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An obsessive gardener grabbing the top of a rosebud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bud' looks horticultural but is the American slang for a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bud is informal US shorthand for buddy, a pal or mate.

clue.text: Mark of Brontë sister, before getting back from the east

indicators.note: reading from the east in an across clue is right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
to back someone is to aid or support them

explanation.surface: A token of one of the Brontë sisters, acquired before being brought home from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brontë sister' wants to be a unit, but the definition is just 'Mark of Brontë', the dots on its e.
explanation.definitionFit: A diaeresis is the two-dot accent placed over a vowel to show it is sounded separately, as on Brontë.

clue.text: Wretch thus adopting tot

indicators.note: adopting takes something in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
to tot up is to add

explanation.surface: A miserable person who therefore takes in a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tot' looks like a child but is the verb, to add up.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddo is British slang for a pathetic, inadequate person, a sorry or contemptible figure.

clue.text: Felt guilt about lacking etiquette in speech

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the word for bad-mannered matches the answer

parts.note: someone without manners is rude

explanation.surface: Someone regretting a breach of manners during a public address.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to regret it, so rued means was sorry for.

clue.text: English writer's pair of jackets from library

indicators.note: a pair means two, so the jacket letters are written down a second time

parts.note: the jackets of a word are its outside letters, wrapped round it like covers on a book, here the first and last of library

explanation.surface: An author owning two dust-jackets borrowed from the library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pair of' doubles the jacket letters, the outside of library, so they appear twice; the 's is 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lyly was an Elizabethan English dramatist and novelist, author of Euphues.

clue.text: Good to break rake, a rotten sort

indicators.note: breaking into something gets inside it

parts.note: a roué is a rake, a dissolute man

explanation.surface: Good, that the rake will snap, since it is a rotten one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rake' suggests a garden tool but means a libertine.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue is a dishonest scoundrel, a bad lot of a person.

clue.text: Delay lob shot, catching one in court

indicators.note: the jumbled letters close around another piece
shot means ruined or broken, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A tennis player delaying a lob, a shot caught on the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' rearranges DELAY LOB, and 'catching' places I inside. 'court' is the tennis one on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Bailey is the Central Criminal Court in London, where major trials are heard.

clue.text: Artist gate-crashing parties for group of stars

indicators.note: a gatecrasher pushes into the party, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a do is a party, so two of them
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A painter sneaking into celebrity parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stars' sounds like celebrities but means real ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorado, the swordfish, is a southern constellation containing the Large Magellanic Cloud.

clue.text: Involved in songs, or did lyrics with some sleaze

indicators.note: the answer is caught up within this run of words

explanation.surface: Someone involved in writing songs whose lyrics were a bit sleazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sordidly means in a sleazy, morally squalid way.
